hook.text: A smoker trying to quit sees cigarettes in every scene of every movie. Nonsmokers never notice.

buildup.text: Our emotions steer our attention. Anxious people spot threats faster than calm people do.

discovery.text: Attentional bias means we focus on stimuli that match our emotional state or current concerns.

twist.text: Hungry people spot food words faster in a word search. The bias is automatic, not chosen.

climax.text: Your emotional state acts like a search filter on reality. You find what you feel.

details.summary: Attentional bias is the tendency to pay more attention to certain types of stimuli while ignoring others, driven by emotional significance, personal relevance, or recent experience. It shapes perception by filtering what enters conscious awareness.
details.whyItMatters: Attentional bias determines what information reaches decision-making processes. People who attend selectively to threats, opportunities, or emotionally charged cues make systematically different decisions than those who scan information more evenly.
takeaways: Emotionally significant stimuli capture attention disproportionately
Attentional bias can create or reinforce anxiety and phobias
What people notice first shapes their interpretation of entire situations

faq.question: How does attentional bias affect everyday decisions?
faq.answer: Investors fixated on recent losses miss growth opportunities. Anxious people notice threats everywhere while ignoring safety cues. Dieters fixate on forbidden foods. The bias creates a skewed information diet that distorts judgment.

faq.question: Can attentional bias be reduced or corrected?
faq.answer: Attentional bias modification training, which redirects attention from threatening to neutral stimuli, shows promise for anxiety disorders. For everyday decisions, deliberately seeking disconfirming information helps counteract natural attentional biases.
